amendments.why: Rule 40 places a preposition the recasting silences and then directs that 'its suffix takes the English pronoun that realizes it, including a subject pronoun'. Both of its examples are cases where the suffix is in fact rendered, so the rule as written does not reach an ethical dative for which the ASV writes nothing at all -- six of them in this chapter, at SNG.2.10 twice, 2.11, 2.13 twice and 2.17. A verse pass reading rule 40 alone is pushed to find a pronoun that is not there, and the nearest tempting word is the phrasal particle standing beside the verb (*Rise up*, *come away*), which rule 44 gives to the verb. The added paragraph states the condition rather than the lemma, so it does not contradict the corpus, which aligns lamed to an English word in thousands of units and includes ASV renderings such as *Get thee out* where the dative suffix does take a pronoun; the corpus's 1139 unrepresented pronominal-suffix units are consistent with it and none contradicts it.
amendments.rule: Where the ASV's recasting leaves a preposition with no English word — the impersonal `קרא לְ` + suffix rendered as a personal passive, `וְקֹרָא לָךְ` → *and thou shalt be called*, or a dative `לְ` + suffix rendered as a bare English indirect object, `תְּנָה לִּי` → *give me* — the preposition is its own `unrepresented` unit and its suffix takes the English pronoun that realizes it, including a subject pronoun. This is rule 21's recasting clause outside the resultative `הָיָה לְ`, and it is the case where rule 18's *possessive or object* is not the whole range. **The `לְ` is the commonest case, not the condition.** The same recasting silences any preposition it leaves nothing to say: `צוּר עַל` → *besieged Tirzah* and `צִוִּיתִי עָלֶיךָ` → *commanded thee* leave `עַל` bare, `אֶל` goes the same way before a bare English object, and a `בְּ` whose object the ASV promotes to a direct object — *blew the trumpet* — keeps nothing either. Read the condition, not the lemma: ask whether the ASV spends an English word on what that preposition contributes. **And a word the ASV writes as part of a neighbouring morpheme's own compound rendering is not a word spent on the preposition.** Where a Hebrew adverb or noun standing beside the preposition is rendered by an English expression written in two or three words, that expression belongs whole to the morpheme it renders, exactly as rule 30 reads its one-English-word condition as one rendering rather than one token, and the preposition takes a word only where the ASV has written one for its own relation. `הֶחָצֵר סָבִיב לַמִּשְׁכָּן` → *the court round about the tabernacle* gives *round about* whole to `סָבִיב`, headed on *round* under rule 24, and leaves the `לְ` `unrepresented`, exactly as the coordinated `וְלַמִּזְבֵּחַ` beside it is left. Do not divide such an expression to give a present preposition something to hold: rule 11 gives each morpheme the English it licenses, and half of another morpheme's fixed rendering is not English this one licenses. Test by subtraction as elsewhere — drop the word and ask whether the preposition's own relation has gone unstated, or whether only the neighbouring expression has been broken in two. The corpus renders `סָבִיב` by *round about* headed on *round* in 144 units and by a bare *round* in two, one of them hedged and the other a doubled adverb for which the ASV writes a separate word for each occurrence, and it reads the whole compound as the adverb's own in four of the five units where a determined preposition follows it. **But read whether the preposition's own object is rendered at all before silencing it.** Every case above is one where the ASV writes English for what the preposition governs and leaves only the relation unstated — *besieged Tirzah*, *commanded thee*, *blew the trumpet*, *give me*, *round about the tabernacle*. Where instead the governed noun is itself left with no English of its own, and a single English word carries the predicate, the preposition and that noun together, rule 30's one-rendering condition is met and this rule does not reach it: the contiguous morphemes share one unit headed on the one carrying the lexeme, rather than one rendered morpheme standing beside others marked `unrepresented`, which is what rule 30 forbids for a fixed expression and what rule 22 forbids for a morpheme whose sense the ASV has written inside a fused word. `אִם־רַע בְּעֵינֶיךָ` → *if it displease thee* gives *it displease* to `רַע`, `בְּ` and `עַיִן` in one unit headed on the verb, while the suffix keeps the *thee* written for it under rule 18, exactly as `הֵשִׁיב פָּנִים` → *deny* fuses under rule 30. Contiguity is that rule's condition and it is the limit here too: `גָּדַל ... מִן` → *exceeded*, where the subject or the object stands between, is split by rule 2 and its preposition is `unrepresented` as before. Test by subtraction — drop the English word and ask whether the preposition's noun as well as its relation has gone unsaid; where the noun keeps a word of its own, this rule governs and the preposition is `unrepresented`. **And where the ASV writes no pronoun for the suffix either, that suffix is its own `unrepresented` unit beside its preposition.** This rule's first sentence places a pronoun the ASV has written; a reflexive or ethical dative the ASV renders by nothing at all — `קוּמִי לָךְ` → *Rise up*, `וּלְכִי־לָךְ` → *and come away*, `הָלַךְ לוֹ` → *is over and gone* — leaves neither morpheme an English word, and each goes `unrepresented` on its own merits under rule 11. Do not read a phrasal particle standing beside the verb as the dative's rendering: *up*, *away* and *forth* are the English verb's own under rule 44, and the subtraction test rules 16 and 43 use finds the verb's rendering diminished when they are dropped while the dative's relation is left unstated either way. Read what the ASV writes rather than the lemma, since the same construction is rendered both ways: where a pronoun is written for the suffix — `לֶךְ־לְךָ` → *Get thee out* — this rule's first sentence governs as before and the suffix takes it.

conventions: The comparative lamed after damah is `unrepresented`: the ASV spends its one word on the verb's own lexeme, as `domeh` -> *is like* and `demeh` -> *be thou like*, so both prepositions of `litzvi o le'ofer` go unrendered, at SNG.2.9 and SNG.2.17 alike. The competing reading gives *like* to the first preposition and only the copula to the verb; it is named in each unit's note and was not taken, because dropping *like* leaves the verb with no rendering at all.

An ethical dative lamed with its suffix -- lakh, lo, lekha -- is rendered by nothing in this chapter, and both morphemes are their own `unrepresented` units: SNG.2.10 twice, SNG.2.11, SNG.2.13 twice, and SNG.2.17. The *up* of *Rise up*, the *away* of *come away* and the *gone* of `halakh lo` -> *is over and gone* are the English verbs' own words under rule 44 and are not the dative's rendering.

`hinneh-zeh` is split rather than fused: the particle takes *behold* and the demonstrative `zeh` takes the English subject pronoun *he*, at SNG.2.8 and SNG.2.9, because the ASV writes a word for each. Where no demonstrative stands beside a participle, the supplied subject pronoun joins the verb's unit under rule 17 instead, as it does for both later participles of SNG.2.9.

In the comparative `ke- X ... ken Y` the fronted preposition takes only *As*, and the verbless clause's one construction-supplied copula joins the correlative `ken`, giving *So is*, at SNG.2.2 and SNG.2.3. The competing reading places that copula on the fronted comparative phrase; it is named in both units' notes and was not taken, because the ASV writes the copula beside the correlative.

`semadar` as the predicate of a verbless clause takes the ASV's whole *are in blossom* -- the construction-supplied copula and the supplied *in* alike -- headed on *blossom*, at SNG.2.13 and SNG.2.15. The supplied preposition is that predicate nominal's own under rule 33 and is not `added`.

A relative the ASV supplies to recast a modifying expression stays with the expression it recasts, while a coordinator the ASV supplies between juxtaposed clauses is `added`. `bechagvei hassela` -> *that art in the clefts of the rock* keeps *that art* with the preposition heading the prepositional predicate at SNG.2.14, and `mechabbelim` -> *That spoil* keeps *That* with the articleless attributive participle at SNG.2.15 under rule 41; the *and* of `chalaf halakh` -> *is over and gone* at SNG.2.11 and of `sov demeh` -> *Turn ... and be thou like* at SNG.2.17 is `added` under rule 14. The 2.14 extension of rule 41's reasoning from an attributive to a prepositional predicate rests on this one occurrence and is recorded here rather than promoted.

report: Checked all 25 candidate lemmas; no cross-verse split. Every multi-treatment bucket is licensed by what the ASV wrote. The article is unrepresented in exactly the phrases with no written *the* (2.1 *a rose of Sharon*, 2.2 *among thorns*, 2.5 *with raisins* and *with apples*, 2.9 and 2.17 *a young hart*) and takes the written *the* everywhere else, including both assimilated bracketed tokens the ASV does render at 2.12 and 2.16. The preposition lamed is aligned only where the ASV writes a word for it (2.3 *to*, 2.10 *unto*); the four comparative lameds of 2.9 and 2.17 and the six ethical datives of 2.10, 2.11, 2.13 and 2.17 are unrepresented on that same ground. The min of 2.9 is *at* then *through* because the ASV wrote both.

The five `added` units, which the lemma table is blind to, were read end to end and hold one coherent line. A coordinator the ASV supplies between clauses the Hebrew juxtaposes is `added`: the *and* of 2.11 for asyndetic chalaf halak, the *and* of 2.17 for asyndetic sov demeh. A supplied nominal or possessive with no morpheme behind it is `added`: *of birds* at 2.12, *their* at 2.13, *his flock* at 2.16. A supplied relative that recasts a modifying expression stays with that expression: *that art in* at 2.14, *That spoil* at 2.15. The apparent tension between the `added` *their* of 2.13 and the *my* handed to the article at 2.7 is licensed by the source, since reyach carries no determiner morpheme and ahavah carries an article.

Article counts across the chapter's construct chains follow rule 29 case by case. The arthrous chains write two determiners and split them: 2.1 *A lily of the valleys*, 2.3 *the trees of the wood*, 2.7 *the hinds of the field*, 2.12 twice, 2.14 twice. 2.4 *the banqueting house* writes a single *the* before an attributively rendered rectum and so fronts it onto the article, leaving the construct bare. The two chains inside 2.1 differ for that reason and not by inconsistency.

Rule 31 heads are uniform: the supplied generic never heads (*apple* tree 2.3, *fig* tree 2.13, *steep* place 2.14, *fair* one 2.10 and 2.13, *left*/*right* hand 2.6), and where the ASV writes the class noun alone elsewhere the head stays on it (*figs* at 2.13, *turtle* at 2.12, *hart* at 2.9 and 2.17). The 2.13 *green figs* call rests on the ASV writing *fig* for te'enah in the same verse, and its note names the competing reading.

The two repeated imperative clauses of 2.10 and 2.13 are aligned identically morpheme for morpheme; the only difference, *Rise up* against *Arise*, is the ASV's own. The parallel comparative predicates of 2.9 and 2.17 are likewise identical.

BSB disagreements: none is a genuine error. The Td x 4, R x 10, Sp2fs x 4 and Sp2ms items are the documented convention difference, BSB attaching an article, a preposition or a dative suffix to its phrase where the ASV writes nothing for it; the 2.7 object marker is rule 16's default reading. The one substantive item, the unrepresented waw at 2.3, is right: the verse holds two waws and one English *And*, and that *And* stands before *his fruit*, which is the second waw's clause, so the first is in surplus under rule 42's counting.

Nothing was changed to improve an aggregate score, and no accepted edge was touched. Six chapter-wide judgments are recorded as conventions; the validation report's 36 repeated notes are otherwise restatements of contract rules and are not logged.
